column12: Instead of just seeing "The Fly" as a scary monster movie, Girard asks us to see it as a classical tragedy, like a story by Shakespeare or the ancient Greeks. When she makes the heartbreaking choice to end his suffering, Girard argues we experience catharsis. Our intense emotions are purged, leaving us with a sense of sad finality. column12: Davies's analysis uses a concept called "topoanalysis," which is just a fancy way of saying we're analyzing a place (in this case, the house) as if it were a mind. Think of the house at 111 Archer Avenue not just as a building, but as a map of the Tenenbaum family's psychology. Davies argues that every part of the house—from the cluttered hallways to the individual, themed bedrooms—symbolizes a specific hang-up or past failure. For example, Chas's childhood room filled with his adult business equipment shows he never emotionally left. Margot's tent-like room reflects her secrecy and isolation. The house itself, with its unchanging decor, traps them in their "child prodigy" pasts, preventing them from growing up. It's less a home and more a beautifully decorated cage built from memory and regret.

column11: Scholar Schmidt attempts to interpret the characters' deadpan performance style using the concept of affective flatness. According to this interpretation, the subdued acting is ultimately revealed to be a defense mechanism against overwhelming melancholy. The lack of overt emotional display is not a sign of emptiness but of a profound, suppressed sadness. This "flat" delivery creates a tension between the absurdity of the situations and the genuine pain underneath, forcing the audience to look for emotion in subtle gestures rather than expressive outbursts.
column12: Schmidt is looking at why the actors in the film seem so emotionless and speak in a monotone, a style we call "deadpan." He uses the term "affective flatness" to describe this. The core idea is that this isn't just a quirky stylistic choice; it's a symptom of the characters' deep, unspoken sadness. Imagine being so overwhelmed by grief or disappointment that you shut down all outward emotional expression as a way to cope. Schmidt argues this is what the Tenenbaums are doing. Their "flat" acting is like a protective shell. It creates a powerful contrast for the viewer: we see ridiculous things happening on screen, but the characters' lack of reaction hints at a very real, very deep pain lurking just beneath the surface.

column4: Renault, Adrien. "Failing the Father: Royal Tenenbaum and the Lacanian Void." Film Criticism 39, no. 2 (2014): 55-72.
column7: Royal Tenenbaum's character arc
column11: Scholar Renault attempts to interpret Royal Tenenbaum's role as the patriarch using the Lacanian concept of the 'Name-of-the-Father.' According to this interpretation, Royal is ultimately revealed to be a failed symbolic father whose absence created a psychic void in his children. His return and attempts to feign illness are a desperate, farcical effort to reinscribe himself as the central authority (the 'Law'), but he can only offer a flawed, human connection, not the symbolic order his children crave, forcing them to finally create their own meaning.
column12: This analysis uses a complex idea from psychoanalyst Jacques Lacan called the "Name-of-the-Father." In simple terms, this isn't about the literal dad, but the idea of the father as the source of rules, order, and identity for a child. Renault argues that Royal completely failed at this job. By abandoning his family, he left a "void"—his children grew up without a strong sense of structure or purpose, which is why they are all stuck as adults. When Royal comes back, he's trying to reclaim that powerful "father" role, but it's too late. He can't just step back in and be the lawgiver. All he can be is a flawed, dying man. The film's resolution, for Renault, is about the children finally realizing they have to build their own lives and identities without relying on this failed father figure.

column4: Miller, T. S. "A Curated Past: Nostalgia and Pastiche in Anderson's Mise-en-Scène." Velvet Light Trap, no. 61 (Spring 2008): 18-29.
column7: The film's hyper-stylized aesthetic (sets, costumes, props)
column11: Scholar Miller attempts to interpret the film's meticulously detailed aesthetic using Fredric Jameson's theory of postmodern pastiche. According to this interpretation, the film's visual style is ultimately revealed to be a "blank parody," a collection of nostalgic signifiers (vintage board games, outdated technology, 70s fashion) detached from their original historical contexts. This creates a world that feels like a museum of a past that never existed, evoking a sense of longing (nostalgia) for an inauthentic time, mirroring the characters' own fixation on their fabricated "genius" pasts.
column12: Miller's argument focuses on the film's unique look—the vintage clothes, old-fashioned electronics, and perfectly arranged rooms. He uses the term "pastiche," which means copying the style of something from the past. However, he argues it's a specific kind of copying called "blank parody." Unlike a regular parody that makes fun of the original, this style just imitates without any critical comment. The result is that the film's world feels like a grab-bag of cool-looking things from the 1970s and 80s, but they're all mixed together in a way that never actually happened. This creates a feeling of "nostalgia for a past that never was." Miller believes this visual strategy perfectly reflects the characters, who are all trapped by nostalgia for their own childhoods, which were also highly artificial and constructed.

column4: Covington, Sarah. "Needle in the Hay: Anempathetic Sound and Affective Rupture." Music, Sound, and the Moving Image 8, no. 1 (2014): 45-61.
column7: Richie Tenenbaum's suicide attempt scene
column11: Scholar Covington attempts to interpret the use of Elliott Smith's "Needle in the Hay" during Richie's suicide attempt using Michel Chion's concept of anempathetic sound. According to this interpretation, the music is ultimately revealed to be indifferent to the on-screen tragedy. Its steady, detached rhythm proceeds impassively as Richie methodically cuts his hair and wrists. This clash between the emotionally charged visuals and the cool, dispassionate music intensifies the horror and isolates Richie's pain, suggesting the world's profound indifference to his suffering.
column12: This analysis focuses on the powerful scene where Richie attempts suicide while Elliott Smith's song "Needle in the Hay" plays. The key concept is "anempathetic sound," a term from film theorist Michel Chion. It describes music that seems completely indifferent or emotionally detached from the drama happening on screen (the opposite of typical dramatic music that swells with emotion). Covington argues that the song's calm, repetitive, and almost clinical tone creates a chilling effect. As we watch Richie's incredibly violent and desperate act, the music just keeps going, as if it doesn't care. This makes the scene even more disturbing. It highlights Richie's feeling of total isolation and makes his personal agony feel even more intense because the soundtrack—and by extension, the world—seems to ignore it completely.

column11: Scholar Peterson attempts to interpret the matching red tracksuits using a semiotic analysis of costume. According to this interpretation, the tracksuits are ultimately revealed to be a form of "character armor" symbolizing Chas's desperate attempt to impose order and control in the wake of his wife's death. The uniform signifies safety, regimentation, and a shared identity, but it also physically marks him and his sons as trapped in a state of perpetual, hyper-vigilant mourning, unable to move beyond their trauma.
column12: Peterson looks at the matching red tracksuits that Chas, Ari, and Uzi wear and asks, "What do they mean?" He uses semiotics, which is the study of signs and symbols. He argues the tracksuits are more than just clothes; they are a symbol, or what he calls "character armor." After his wife's death, Chas becomes obsessed with safety and order. By putting himself and his sons in a uniform, he's trying to create a controlled, predictable little unit to protect them from the chaos of the world. However, the bright, unchanging uniform also becomes a visual sign of their trauma. It shows they are stuck in a cycle of grief and anxiety, unable to relax or be individuals. The tracksuit is both a shield and a cage.

column7: Margot Tenenbaum's characterization as "the adopted daughter"
column11: Scholar Cho attempts to interpret Margot's persistent otherness within the family using Laura Mulvey's concept of the male gaze. According to this interpretation, Margot is ultimately revealed to be an objectified spectacle whose identity is constantly defined by the men around her—Royal's introduction, Richie's romantic obsession, Raleigh's scientific observation. Her secrecy, chain-smoking, and hidden life are not mere quirks but acts of rebellion against a patriarchal gaze that seeks to contain and understand her, representing her struggle for an autonomous identity.
column12: Cho analyzes the character of Margot, focusing on how she's always introduced as "the adopted daughter." She uses a famous feminist film theory concept called the "male gaze," which describes how women in film are often presented as passive objects to be looked at by male characters and the audience. Cho argues that Margot is constantly being defined by the men in her life. Her father introduces her by listing her secrets, her brother Richie idealizes and desires her, and her husband Raleigh studies her like a lab rat. Her whole identity is shaped by their "gaze." Cho sees Margot's secret life—her smoking, her affairs, her past—as a form of resistance. It's her way of having a self that the men in her life can't see, control, or define.

column7: The film's literary structure and omniscient narrator
column11: Scholar Wexler attempts to interpret the film's storybook structure and omniscient narrator using Wayne Booth's concept of the 'implied author.' According to this interpretation, the narrator is ultimately revealed to be a curated, fictional persona of the director himself, not a neutral storyteller. This "narrator-auteur" presents the family's history with a mix of encyclopedic detail and ironic detachment, shaping our perception of events. The literary format (chapters, prologue) reinforces the idea that we are receiving a constructed, authored, and therefore unreliable, version of the Tenenbaums' "true" story.
column12: This analysis focuses on how the film is told like a book, with chapters and a narrator (voiced by Alec Baldwin) who seems to know everything. Wexler uses the literary idea of an "implied author," which suggests that behind the narrator, there's a sense of the real author's personality and biases. He argues that the narrator isn't just telling us the story; he's crafting it with a specific, witty, and slightly sad point of view that is basically Wes Anderson's own style. The narrator's god-like knowledge and deadpan delivery make the story feel both epic and a little bit fake. This reminds the audience that what they're seeing isn't reality, but a carefully constructed, almost mythical version of the Tenenbaum family's life, as told by a very particular storyteller.

column7: Pig Sty Alley community and its destruction
column11: Scholar Szeto attempts to interpret Pig Sty Alley and its struggle against the Axe Gang using historiographical allegory. According to this interpretation, the Target Object is ultimately revealed to be a microcosm of Hong Kong's history, representing the pre-1997 Kowloon Walled City, a space of both community and lawlessness. The Axe Gang symbolizes encroaching colonial and later mainland Chinese authority, with the battle over the alley allegorizing Hong Kong's struggle to maintain its unique identity against larger political forces.
column12: This analysis suggests Pig Sty Alley isn't just a random poor neighborhood. Think of it as a symbolic representation of a real, famous place in Hong Kong's past: the Kowloon Walled City. This place was known for its strong sense of community, separate from British colonial rule. Szeto argues that the Axe Gang, with their sharp suits and organized crime, represent larger, outside forces trying to take over – first the British, and later, by implication, the mainland Chinese government after the 1997 handover. So, the whole fight for the alley is a movie-sized metaphor for Hong Kong's real-life struggle to keep its own culture and way of life.

column4: Chan, Felicia. "The international articulation of a blockbuster: Stephen Chow’s Kung Fu Hustle." Journal of Chinese Cinemas 2, no. 2 (2008): 101-114.
column7: The film's blend of wuxia tropes and Hollywood special effects/genres (e.g., Looney Tunes, The Matrix)
column11: Scholar Chan attempts to interpret the film's aesthetic fusion of local Hong Kong cinema and global Hollywood styles using the concept of glocalization. According to this interpretation, the Target Object is ultimately revealed to be a calculated product designed for transnational appeal. By embedding universally recognized cinematic language (like CGI-heavy action and cartoon physics) within a specific cultural context (the wuxia genre and 1940s Shanghai), the film "articulates" itself to both domestic and international audiences, maximizing its blockbuster potential.
column12: Imagine you're trying to sell a product worldwide. You must adapt it. That's what "glocalization" means – thinking globally, but acting locally. Chan argues that *Kung Fu Hustle* does exactly this. It takes a local Hong Kong flavor – the kung fu (wuxia) stories – and mixes it with things everyone around the world understands from Hollywood movies. Think of the crazy, physics-defying chases that look like a Road Runner cartoon, or the slow-motion fight scenes that remind you of *The Matrix*. By blending these two worlds, Stephen Chow made a film that felt familiar and exciting to people in China and America, making it a true global blockbuster.

column7: Sing's character arc from a wannabe gangster to the ultimate martial artist
column11: Scholar Yip attempts to interpret Sing's transformation using the framework of neoliberal subjectivity. According to this interpretation, Sing's journey is not just about finding his inner hero, but about becoming an ideal neoliberal subject. He begins as a failed entrepreneur of crime, seeking individual profit. His "true self" is only unlocked through extreme competition and a near-death experience, re-emerging as an all-powerful individual whose skills privatize justice and restore order. His final act is not joining a community, but opening a candy shop—a small business owner.
column12: This is a bit complex, but think about the values our society often promotes: be your own boss, work hard to get ahead, be an individual entrepreneur. This is part of an economic idea called "neoliberalism." Yip argues that Sing's story fits this mold perfectly. He's a failed con artist until a "trial by fire" makes him the best. But what does he do with his power? He doesn't start a school. He defeats the bad guy (eliminating the competition) and then opens a small candy store. He becomes the ultimate successful individual entrepreneur, a perfect hero for our modern, business-focused times.

column4: Pang, Laikwan. "The state of the popular, or, the popular and the state in contemporary Chinese cinema." Screen 55, no. 1 (2014): 46-65.
column7: The film's ending where Sing renounces violence and opens a lollipop shop
column11: Scholar Pang attempts to interpret the film's ending through the concept of "minjian" (the popular, the grassroots, the non-state). According to this interpretation, Sing's final rejection of the kung fu world is a deliberate counter-narrative to state-sponsored heroic epics. While official Chinese cinema often co-opts martial arts heroes for nationalist purposes, Sing's return to simple, everyday life and small-scale capitalism (the candy store) represents a retreat into the private, apolitical "minjian" sphere, subtly resisting ideological appropriation by the state.
column12: In China, there's a difference between official government-approved culture ("the state") and the culture of regular people ("minjian"). Pang points out that the government often uses big martial arts movies to promote national pride. But in *Kung Fu Hustle*, the hero becomes the most powerful fighter in the world and then gives it all up to run a candy store. Pang argues this is a meaningful choice. It's the film saying that true happiness isn't in grand, heroic acts, but in the small, simple, private world of ordinary people – the "minjian" world. It’s a quiet form of rebellion against being used for state propaganda.

column7: The character of "The Beast" and his fight scenes
column11: Scholar Szeto attempts to interpret the character of The Beast by analyzing him as a postmodern pastiche. According to this interpretation, The Beast is not a singular character but a collage of cinematic references. He wears a suit like an agent from *The Matrix*, has the unkempt look of a classic kung fu villain, can stop a bullet like Superman, and employs the Toad Style from old Shaw Brothers films. This "blank parody" mixes and matches historical and pop culture signifiers without a clear critical target, creating a spectacle that celebrates film history itself.
column12: "Pastiche" is like making a collage, but with styles instead of pictures. Szeto argues that the main villain, "The Beast," is a perfect example. He's a mix-and-match of many other villains. He looks a bit like an agent from *The Matrix*, he can stop a bullet like Superman, and his "Toad Style" fighting move is a direct reference to old-school kung fu movies. The film isn't making fun of these other movies (that would be parody); instead, it's just playfully borrowing all these cool styles and putting them together to create something new and fun. It's a celebration of all the movies that came before it.

column11: Scholar Yeh interprets the casting of veteran actors from the golden age of kung fu cinema through the lens of spectral nostalgia. According to this interpretation, these actors are not just playing roles; they are "ghosts" or specters of a bygone era of Hong Kong cinema. Their presence haunts the film, evoking a sense of loss for the authentic, physical martial arts style and the local industry that has been superseded by CGI and global co-productions. They represent a lost past that the film both lovingly resurrects and confirms is gone forever.
column12: Nostalgia is that warm feeling you get for the past. This analysis uses a more specific idea: "spectral nostalgia," where the past feels like a ghost that haunts the present. Yeh argues that Stephen Chow intentionally cast actors who were big stars in 1970s kung fu movies. When audiences who grew up with those old movies see these actors, it's like seeing ghosts from a "golden age" of Hong Kong film. Their presence reminds us of a time before computer effects, when action felt more "real." The film is both a loving tribute to that past and a sad reminder that it's gone for good, replaced by a new, global style of filmmaking.

column7: The "Musical Number" scene where the Axe Gang dances
column11: Scholar Williams interprets the Axe Gang's dance sequence as a prime example of the film's generic hybridity. According to this interpretation, the scene abruptly shatters the established tone of a martial arts film by injecting conventions from the Hollywood musical. This blending of seemingly incompatible genres—gangster film, kung fu, and musical comedy—is a key strategy of Stephen Chow's "mo lei tau" (nonsensical) comedy. It serves to deconstruct audience expectations and create a comedic spectacle that operates on a level of pure cinematic pleasure rather than narrative coherence.
column12: Most movies stick to one main category, or "genre," like comedy or action. Williams focuses on how *Kung Fu Hustle* loves to mix genres in surprising ways ("generic hybridity"). Think about the scene where the Axe Gang, who are supposed to be scary gangsters, suddenly break into a choreographed dance number. For a moment, the gangster movie turns into a Hollywood musical. This is a classic element of Stephen Chow's unique comedy style, called "mo lei tau" or "nonsensical." By throwing in a dance number, he's playing with our expectations, making us laugh by breaking the rules of how a kung fu movie is "supposed" to work.

This reading reveals the housing project not as a location, but as a modern haunted castle where architectural decay and social neglect manifest as supernatural terror. The neglected high-rise replaces the crumbling manor, its dark corridors and graffiti-covered walls becoming repositories of repressed social anxieties and violent histories that give birth to a monster.
column12: The Urban Gothic theory updates classic Gothic horror ideas (like spooky castles) for a modern city setting. Think of Cabrini-Green not just as a poor neighborhood, but as a giant, decaying castle. Fhlainn's analysis shows how the building's physical state—broken windows, dark hallways, graffiti—reflects the social decay and neglect of its residents. The horror isn't just a ghost; it's born from the very real trauma and history embedded in the architecture itself. Candyman is the "ghost in the machine" of a failed social project.

Instead, they fester and come back in monstrous forms. Wood's theory would see Candyman as the physical manifestation of America's repressed history of lynching and racial violence. column11: Cherry interprets Helen's transformation using Kristeva's theory of abjection, as filtered through Creed's monstrous-feminine. column12: Abjection is our psychological horror of things that threaten our sense of a clean, proper self (like blood, decay, or corpses). Barbara Creed applied this to horror films, arguing they often present women as "monstrous-feminine" when they are associated with these abject things. Cherry's analysis shows Helen's journey is a process of becoming abject. She starts as a clean academic, but is progressively covered in blood and grime, losing her place in society. Ultimately, she fully transforms, crossing the line from human to monster, becoming a new urban legend herself.

Candyman's curse is a violent rejection of this gaze, forcing the observer to become the observed and a victim of the very story she sought to control.

column11: Brown interprets Philip Glass's minimalist score through the lens of musical hauntology. According to this interpretation, the score's repetitive, cyclical nature, combining a grand organ with a haunting choir, functions not as typical horror music but as a sonic ghost. It represents the persistent, unresolved trauma of the past—a "failed future" of racial harmony—that now haunts the present architectural and social landscape of Chicago, musically echoing Candyman's own spectral persistence.
column12: Hauntology is the idea that the present is haunted by the "ghosts" of lost futures. In music, this means a sound that feels nostalgic for a future that never happened. Brown's analysis suggests Philip Glass's score does this for Candyman. The grand, almost religious-sounding music (organ, choir) feels out of place in a run-down housing project. It sonically represents the ghost of Daniel Robitaille's cultured, aspirational life and the promise of a post-racial society that was violently destroyed. The music is the "haunting" echo of that lost potential.

column11: Elliott interprets the ritual of saying Candyman's name using the concept of semiotic rupture. According to this interpretation, the act of vocalizing the name is more than a superstition; it is a performative act that collapses the boundary between symbol (the name) and reality (the monster). It represents the power of oral history, suppressed by official written discourse like Helen's thesis, to physically manifest and disrupt the present, forcing a reckoning with history.
column12: Semiotics is the study of signs and symbols. A "semiotic rupture" is a moment when the connection between a sign (a word, an image) and its meaning breaks down or becomes dangerously real. Elliott's analysis argues that saying "Candyman" five times causes such a rupture. The name ceases to be just a word in a story and becomes a trigger that makes the story real. This gives power to oral storytelling, the way legends are passed down in communities, showing it to be more powerful and dangerous than the "safe," written analysis Helen is trying to produce.

column11: Pinedo's postmodern horror framework can be used to interpret Helen's arc as a Final Girl trope inversion. Unlike the traditional Final Girl who survives by defeating the monster and reaffirming social norms (often through her moral purity), Helen survives by *becoming* the monster. Her final act is not one of purification or escape, but of embracing monstrosity to enact vengeful justice, thereby subverting the slasher genre's typically conservative ideology.
column12: The "Final Girl," a concept from Carol Clover, is the last character standing in a horror movie, usually a resourceful, virginal young woman who defeats the killer. Pinedo's theory looks at how '90s horror plays with these old rules. Helen's story is an inversion of the trope. She doesn't kill the monster to restore order. Instead, she joins him in death and myth. She survives not as a person, but as a new monster, a vengeful ghost who carries on the cycle of violence. This is a much darker and more critical ending than a classic slasher film.

column7: The character of Bernadette "Bernie" Walsh
column11: Warner's analysis would interpret Bernadette's character using the Sacrificial Black Character Trope. According to this interpretation, Bernie functions primarily to voice caution to the white protagonist (Helen) and then dies gruesomely to demonstrate the stakes and motivate Helen's plot. Her death, while shocking, serves to center the narrative on the white character's experience and trauma, reinforcing a racial hierarchy common within the horror genre where Black characters are often expendable.
column12: This theory examines a recurring pattern in movies, especially horror, where a Black character's main purpose is to support the white lead and then die. This death often serves as a warning or a catalyst for the white character's emotional journey. Warner's analysis would position Bernadette perfectly within this trope. She is intelligent and sensible, constantly warning Helen about the dangers of her research. Her brutal murder is not about her own story, but about escalating the threat to Helen and pushing her narrative forward, making Bernie a tool in Helen's story rather than a character in her own right.

column4: Nama, Adilifu. "The New Black Horror Film." In Black Space: Imagining Race in Science Fiction Film, 81-108. University of Texas Press, 2008.
column7: Candyman's origin story (Daniel Robitaille)
column11: Nama interprets Candyman's origin story through the lens of the specter of miscegenation. According to this reading, Candyman's monstrosity is born directly from the historical terror surrounding interracial desire in America. His brutal lynching for loving a white woman transforms him into a figure of vengeance whose entire existence is a supernatural manifestation of the violent consequences of transgressing racial taboos. His haunting of Helen is thus a tragic, ghostly reenactment of this forbidden love.
column12: "Miscegenation" is an outdated, offensive term for interracial relationships, and the "specter" of it refers to the deep-seated historical fear and paranoia, particularly in America, about it. Nama's analysis shows that Candyman isn't just a random monster; his origin is rooted in this specific racial trauma. He was an artist, Daniel Robitaille, murdered by a lynch mob. His transformation into a monster is a direct result of this racist violence. Therefore, his return as a murderous ghost is not random evil, but the vengeful specter of this specific, ugly part of American history.

column4: Jones, Steve. "The body and the abject in the new extremism of French cinema." Studies in French Cinema 12, no. 3 (2012): 229-242.
column11: Scholar Jones attempts to interpret Lucie's visions of the creature using the concept of the Abject. According to this interpretation, the creature is not a supernatural ghost but the abjected manifestation of Lucie's own past trauma and self-loathing, a corporeal reminder of the defiled self she is trying to expel. It represents the breakdown of the boundary between self and other, subject and object.
column12: "The abject" refers to things our minds and bodies expel to maintain a sense of a clean, stable self, like waste or a corpse. Jones argues that the scarred creature Lucie sees isn't a real ghost, but a psychological projection embodying her unbearable trauma and self-hatred from her torture. She has "abjected" this part of herself, pushing it away, but it keeps returning to haunt her. The creature is the horrifying physical manifestation of her own damaged body and psyche that she cannot escape, representing the collapse of the border between what is "me" and "not-me."

column4: Firestone, Chris D. "Making Martyrs: The Cinematic Soteriology of Pascal Laugier." Journal of Religion & Film 17, no. 1 (2013): Article 34.
column11: Scholar Firestone attempts to interpret Anna's final state of transcendence using the concept of Atheological Soteriology. According to this interpretation, the film presents a path to salvation (soteriology) that is completely divorced from God or traditional religion. Anna's martyrdom, induced through extreme suffering, achieves a form of insight or 'gnosis' into the nature of existence, but it is a purely material, physiological transcendence, a revelation found within the body's absolute limit, not from a divine power.
column12: "Soteriology" is the study of salvation, and "atheological" means without God. Firestone analyzes how the film creates a version of "salvation" separate from religion. He argues the secret society believes that by pushing the human body to its absolute breaking point, they can trigger a purely biological state of transcendence—a glimpse beyond death. Anna's final, catatonic vision is not a holy revelation in a religious sense; it is a physiological event, a secret unlocked by pushing the body past its limits, a form of knowledge gained through extreme, material experience rather than faith.

column4: Rees-Roberts, Nick. "The Terrorist's Body: Masculinity, Abjection and the New French Extremism." French Screen Studies 13, no. 1 (2013): 67-81.
column11: Scholar Rees-Roberts attempts to interpret the systematic torture within the context of New French Extremity using the concept of the Biopolitical Body. According to this interpretation, the secret society's project treats Anna's body not as a person but as a biological specimen to be managed and pushed to its limits for the extraction of data—in this case, knowledge of the afterlife. This reflects a contemporary anxiety about biopower, where life itself is administered and controlled by quasi-scientific, sovereign powers.
column12: "Biopolitics" describes how modern states or powerful groups manage populations by controlling their bodies (e.g., through public health). Rees-Roberts applies this to the film's secret society, which acts like a state or a laboratory. They don't see Anna as a human; they see her as a "biopolitical body," a biological machine from which they can extract a specific product: information about transcendence. The cold, systematic, and almost medical way they torture her exemplifies this dehumanizing control over life itself, reducing a person to a set of biological processes to be manipulated for data.

column4: Paszkiewicz, Katarzyna. "Female bodies of evidence: New French Extremity in Dans ma peau, High Tension and Martyrs." Studies in European Cinema 9, no. 1 (2012): 35-46.
column11: Scholar Paszkiewicz attempts to interpret the exclusive selection of female victims using the lens of Corporeal Feminism. According to this interpretation, the film critiques the historical tendency in philosophy and horror to view the female body as a passive vessel for suffering and a privileged site for accessing "truth." The cult's belief that only women can become true martyrs ironically reinforces this patriarchal notion, making the film a meta-commentary on the gendered representation of bodily endurance and pain.
column12: "Corporeal Feminism" is a feminist theory focused on the body's experience and representation. Paszkiewicz uses it to question why the cult *only* tortures women. She argues the film is exposing an old, sexist idea: that women are somehow "better" at suffering, more passive, or closer to the spiritual world. The cult's "scientific" project is revealed to be built on this misogynistic myth. By showing this extreme process applied only to female bodies, the film forces the audience to confront how often the female body is used in stories, especially horror, as a vehicle for pain, suffering, and spiritual revelation.

column4: Shaw, Daniel. "The Ghost in the Machine: The Mind-Body Problem in the ‘New Extremism’ of French Horror Cinema." Horror Studies 2, no. 2 (2011): 203-215.
column11: Scholar Shaw attempts to interpret Lucie's self-mutilation using the concept of Post-Traumatic Reenactment. According to this interpretation, Lucie's acts of self-harm, seemingly prompted by the hallucinatory creature, are a compulsive repetition of her original unresolved trauma. The creature represents the internalized torturer, and by cutting herself, Lucie is unconsciously re-staging the original violence in a desperate attempt to gain mastery over a traumatic experience that has collapsed the distinction between her mind and her body.
column12: Trauma theory explains that people who experience horrific events often unconsciously "reenact" them. Shaw applies this to Lucie, arguing that the creature is the living memory of her torturer. When the creature "attacks" her, her mind is forcing a traumatic flashback. Her response—cutting herself—is a tragic, unconscious attempt to control the uncontrollable. It's a psychological loop where her brain thinks, "The original pain was done *to* me, but this time *I* am the one causing it, so I am in charge." She keeps inflicting violence on her own body to try and process the past.

column4: Haladyn, Julian Jason. "Exceptional Suffering: The Case of Pascal Laugier’s Martyrs." Senses of Cinema, no. 55 (2010).
column11: Scholar Haladyn attempts to interpret Mademoiselle's suicide using the concept of The Incommunicable. According to this interpretation, Anna's whispered revelation is not a clear message but a truth that fundamentally resists language and comprehension. Mademoiselle's suicide is a response to the confrontation with this absolute limit of knowledge. The "truth" is either so horrifying (pure nothingness) or so transcendent that it renders normal existence meaningless, representing an experience that cannot be shared, only undergone.
column12: This analysis focuses on the limits of language. Haladyn suggests that whatever Anna experienced is "incommunicable"—it literally cannot be expressed in words. When Anna whispers to Mademoiselle, she isn't just describing a scene. The experience itself is so profound it shatters the listener. Mademoiselle kills herself not because the news is simply "bad" (e.g., "there's nothing") or "good" (e.g., "heaven is real"), but because the *nature* of the knowledge is so overwhelming that it breaks her reality and makes continued existence pointless. The secret isn't the point; the fact that it is unspeakable is.

column4: Haywood, Alice L. "Suffering, Sensation, and the ‘Ethical’ in New Extremist Cinema: The Case of Martyrs." Film-Philosophy 20, no. 2-3 (2016): 331-346.
column11: Scholar Haywood attempts to interpret the audience's reaction to the torture scenes using the concept of Haptic Visuality. According to this interpretation, the film's cinematography and sound design are engineered to make the viewer feel as though they are touching or being touched by the on-screen violence. The close-ups on skin and the raw sound of impacts collapse the distance between spectator and victim, creating an affective, sensory experience that poses an ethical challenge to the act of watching.
column12: "Haptic" means related to the sense of touch. "Haptic Visuality" is a film studies term for when a movie makes you feel like you are physically touching what you see. Haywood argues that *Martyrs* does this intentionally during its torture scenes. The camera stays uncomfortably close, focusing on skin, wounds, and textures, while the sound design is raw and immediate. The intended effect is that you don't just *see* Anna suffer; you almost *feel* it on a physical, gut level. This bypasses intellectual analysis and becomes a direct, sensory assault, forcing you to question the ethics of why you are continuing to watch.

column4: Creed, Barbara. The Monstrous-Feminine: Film, Feminism, Psychoanalysis. Routledge, 1993.
column7: Claire Niveau's body and reproductive organs
column11: Creed interprets Claire Niveau through the psychoanalytic concept of the Archaic Mother, a terrifying, pre-Oedipal maternal figure associated with the abject. According to this interpretation, Claire's 'mutant' womb positions her not as a romantic partner, but as the monstrous maternal origin that threatens to re-absorb the symbiotically-linked twins into a horrifying, undifferentiated state from which they never fully escaped.
column12: The theorist Barbara Creed builds on Julia Kristeva's ideas to propose the "Archaic Mother" as a key figure in horror films. This isn't a loving mother, but a primal, all-encompassing maternal force that existed before we developed our sense of self. It represents a terrifying state of boundary-lessness. Creed argues that the Mantle twins, who are already psychologically merged, perceive Claire's unique anatomy as the ultimate symbol of this Archaic Mother. Her body is not just different; it's a gateway back to the pre-birth fusion they secretly crave and overtly fear. Their obsession with 'curing' her is really a desperate fight against being consumed by this maternal horror.

column4: Shaviro, Steven. The Cinematic Body. University of Minnesota Press, 1993.
column7: The twins' physical and psychological disintegration, including drug abuse and self-surgery
column11: Shaviro analyzes the twins' descent into addiction and mutual destruction using the Deleuzian concept of the Body without Organs. According to this interpretation, their radical, painful attempts to alter their bodies through drugs and surgery are revealed to be a desperate, failed flight from the constraints of their organized, disciplined identities toward a new, non-hierarchical state of pure sensation and intensity.
column12: French philosophers Deleuze and Guattari came up with the idea of the "Body without Organs" (BwO). Imagine your body not as an organized system (heart, lungs, etc.) but as a plane of pure potential and sensation, before it's all defined. Shaviro argues that the Mantle twins are trying to achieve this state. They are trapped in their highly structured lives as successful doctors. Their drug use, their bizarre surgeries, and their eventual merging are not just self-destruction; they are a violent attempt to break down their 'organized' bodies and escape into a BwO—a state of pure, undifferentiated connection. It's a painful, catastrophic process of becoming something new, even if that something is death.

column4: Clover, Carol J. Men, Women, and Chain Saws: Gender in the Modern Horror Film. Princeton University, 1992.
column7: The final "separation" surgery scene where Beverly kills Elliot, and then himself
column11: Clover interprets the film's climax, particularly Beverly's role, through the lens of masochistic identification, a phenomenon she associates with the "Final Girl" in slasher films. According to this interpretation, the final, agonizing scene where Beverly mutilates Elliot is revealed to be a moment where the male protagonist fully occupies the traditionally feminized position of the suffering, abject victim, inviting a cross-gender identification from the audience with his pain and terror.
column12: In her famous book, Carol Clover argued that in slasher films, the male audience ends up identifying with the terror and pain of the female victim (the "Final Girl"). She calls this "masochistic identification." Clover applies this idea to *Dead Ringers*, a film with male victims. She suggests that in the horrifying final scene, we are forced to identify with Beverly. He is not a powerful hero but a terrified, suffering, "feminized" character. The camera puts us right there with him in his agony as he performs the fatal surgery. The film thus subverts typical gender roles in horror, making its male protagonists the ultimate victims we are meant to identify with in their pain.

column4: Adams, Parveen. The Emptiness of the Image: Psychoanalysis and Sexual Differences. Routledge, 1996.
column7: The twins' symbiotic, undifferentiated relationship
column11: Adams analyzes the twins' codependent identity using Jacques Lacan's concept of the Imaginary order, the pre-linguistic psychic realm of fusion and identification best exemplified by the mirror stage. According to this interpretation, the Mantle twins are revealed to be pathologically arrested in this pre-Oedipal dyad. They are unable to fully separate and enter the Symbolic order (the world of language, law, and distinct identity), leading inevitably to their shared psychosis and death when an external force (Claire) threatens their closed circuit.
column12: The psychoanalyst Jacques Lacan described three stages of our psychological development: the Imaginary, the Symbolic, and the Real. The Imaginary is the earliest stage, like when a baby sees itself in a mirror and forms a sense of a whole self, but it's also a stage of being merged with the mother. Adams argues the Mantle twins are trapped in this Imaginary stage. They are each other's mirror image, a perfectly closed loop. They share women, thoughts, and even their sense of self. Claire's arrival threatens this fusion because she forces them to see themselves as separate individuals. Their inability to enter the "Symbolic" world of separate identities leads them to violently regress and destroy themselves.

column4: Doane, Mary Ann. "Technophilia: Technology, Representation, and the Feminine." In Femmes Fatales: Feminism, Film Theory, Psychoanalysis. Routledge, 1991.
column7: The specially designed "Gynecological Instruments for Operating on Mutant Women"
column11: Doane examines Beverly's creation of the bizarre surgical instruments through the concept of technophilia, the obsessive love of technology. According to this interpretation, the strange, archaic-looking metal tools are revealed to be fetish objects. They represent a pathological fusion of a male technological fantasy with a deep-seated anxiety about the female reproductive body. The instruments are designed to probe and control what the twins perceive as the monstrous otherness of women's interiors.
column12: Mary Ann Doane explores the relationship between technology and the representation of women in film. She uses the term "technophilia" to describe an obsessive fascination with technology, often as a way to manage anxieties. In *Dead Ringers*, Beverly's strange, claw-like surgical tools are a perfect example. Doane suggests these are not just medical instruments; they are fetish objects. They embody the twins' desperate, and ultimately perverse, desire to use technology to understand and control the female body, which they see as alien and "mutant." The tools are a physical manifestation of their fear and obsession, a way to impose a cold, metallic logic onto the messiness of biology.

column4: McLarty, Lianne. "The Reproducing Body: The Unutopian in Cronenberg's Dead Ringers." Canadian Journal of Film Studies 1, no. 1 (1990): 57-71.
column7: The "trifurcated cervix" of Claire Niveau
column11: McLarty interprets the twins' fixation on Claire's mutated reproductive organs through Julia Kristeva's theory of the abject—that which is violently cast out from the self to create identity. According to this interpretation, the "trifurcated cervix" is revealed to be a cinematic symbol of the abject maternal body. It is the horrifying, fascinating, and boundary-threatening origin point that jeopardizes the brothers' fragile, shared masculine identity.
column12: Julia Kristeva's concept of the "abject" refers to things we expel from ourselves to form a clean sense of "me"—like bodily fluids, decay, or a corpse. The most primary abject, she argues, is the maternal body, which we must separate from to become an individual. McLarty argues that Claire's unusual anatomy functions as the ultimate abject for the Mantle twins. They are both horrified and fascinated by it because it represents the messy, uncontrollable reality of biological reproduction. Their obsession with "fixing" her is a symbolic attempt to control the primal maternal power that threatens to dissolve their own weak, merged identities.

column4: Hurley, Kelly. The Gothic Body: Sexuality, Materialism, and Degeneration at the Fin de Siècle. Cambridge University Press, 1996.
column7: The Mantle twins' regression from elite surgeons to primitive, drug-addled figures
column11: Hurley reads the twins' downfall through the framework of late-Victorian Gothic degeneration theory, which posited that individuals or races could devolve to a more primitive state. According to this interpretation, the brothers' spectacular regression from the pinnacle of medical science to blood-soaked primitives is revealed to be a modern re-staging of the Gothic fear of atavism—the anxiety that civilization is merely a thin veneer over a monstrous, primal, and inescapable biology.
column12: In the late 19th century, there was a widespread fear called "degeneration"—the idea that humans could biologically and morally regress, devolving into a more "primitive" state. This became a common theme in Gothic horror novels like *Dracula* and *Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde*. Kelly Hurley argues that Cronenberg's films, especially *Dead Ringers*, are modern versions of this Gothic anxiety. The Mantle twins start as the ultimate symbols of modern, civilized man: brilliant surgeons. Their slow descent into drug-fueled madness and squalor is a classic degeneration narrative, showing their "higher" rational selves being consumed by their "lower" primal biology and shared psychosis.

column4: McCallum, E. L. "Mapping the Cinematic Body onto the Medical Body: The Case of 'Dead Ringers'." Screen 38, no. 2 (1997): 129-46.
column7: The film's repeated scenes of gynecological surgery and examination
column11: McCallum interprets the film's clinical scenes using Michel Foucault's concept of the "medical gaze," a dehumanizing way of seeing that separates the patient's body from their identity. According to this interpretation, Cronenberg's camera mimics this gaze, focusing on the female body's interior via medical technology. This is revealed to be an exercise of disciplinary power, transforming the body from a subjective person into a passive, knowable object to be dissected and controlled.
column12: The philosopher Michel Foucault wrote about the "medical gaze," which is how modern medicine learned to see the body as a machine made of parts, separate from the person's identity. It's a powerful but dehumanizing perspective. McCallum argues that Cronenberg's camera in *Dead Ringers* adopts this exact gaze. When we see the internal shots of surgery or the cold, detached way the twins examine Claire, the film isn't just showing us a medical procedure. It is showing us a particular way of seeing that objectifies and controls the female body. The film's horror comes from showing how this supposedly objective medical gaze is actually deeply tied to the twins' psychological obsessions and desire for power.

column4: Ramsay, Christine. "Dead Ringers and the Pathological Public Sphere." Canadian Journal of Film Studies 11, no. 1 (2002): 22-41.
column7: The architectural design of the Mantle clinic and operating theater
column11: Ramsay analyzes the film's cold, sterile spaces by inverting Habermas's concept of the public sphere (a space for rational debate) into a "pathological public sphere." According to this interpretation, the hyper-rational, minimalist design of the clinic and operating theater is revealed to be, not a space of healing, but a public stage. It's an arena where the twins' private, internal psychopathology is externalized, aestheticized, and violently enacted upon the bodies of their female patients.
column12: The theorist Jürgen Habermas described the "public sphere" as an ideal place where private citizens could come together for rational public debate (like an 18th-century coffee house). Christine Ramsay takes this idea and twists it to create the "pathological public sphere." She argues that the Mantle twins' clinic is just such a space. On the surface, it looks like the height of reason and science with its clean lines and sterile environment. But in reality, it's a public theater where their private madness is performed. They use the language and tools of science not to heal, but to act out their perverse obsessions, turning a public space of care into a stage for their pathology.

column4: Wierzbicki, James. "Sister, Sister: The Underscoring of Abnormality in The Other and Dead Ringers." In Film Music: A History. Routledge, 2009.
column7: Howard Shore's musical score, especially the main theme
column11: Wierzbicki analyzes Howard Shore's score through the Freudian concept of the uncanny (Unheimlich), the unsettling experience of the familiar becoming strange. According to this interpretation, the haunting, string-heavy main theme is revealed to be a musical manifestation of the uncanny. Its elegant, classical melody feels familiar, yet it is rendered deeply disturbing by its orchestration and melancholic harmony, perfectly mirroring the twins' relationship—they are an identical, familiar unit made monstrous by their inability to separate.
column12: Sigmund Freud defined the "uncanny" (or *unheimlich* in German) as the feeling of dread that comes from something that is familiar yet somehow strange or out of place. It's the "un-homely" feeling. Wierzbicki argues that Howard Shore's famous musical theme for *Dead Ringers* is a perfect example of the musical uncanny. The melody itself is beautiful and sounds a bit like a classical lullaby (something familiar and comforting). However, the way it's played by the strings—full of sorrow and a subtle dissonance—makes it incredibly unsettling and creepy. The music makes us feel the same way we feel about the twins: they look normal and familiar, but something is profoundly and horrifyingly wrong.

column4: Davies, Lincoln. "The Past is Another Country Song: Linklater's Sonic Historiography." Music, Sound, and the Moving Image 12, no. 1 (2018): 45-68.
column7: The film's classic rock soundtrack
column11: Davies attempts to interpret a specific aspect of the film's soundtrack using the concept of Anempathetic Music. According to this interpretation, the ubiquitous classic rock score is ultimately revealed to be indifferent to the teenagers' minor dramas, creating an ironic distance and highlighting the unchanging, monumental nature of the music against the fleeting anxieties of youth, thereby historicizing the moment rather than merely sentimentalizing it.
column12: This analysis looks at how the music works in the film. Imagine a sad scene, but a happy, upbeat rock song like Aerosmith's "Sweet Emotion" is playing. The theorist Michel Chion calls this "anempathetic music"—sound that shows a clear indifference to the on-screen action. Scholar Davies argues that Linklater uses this technique deliberately. The constant rock'n'roll doesn't care about the characters' breakups or worries. This makes the music feel like a historical artifact, a permanent part of the 1970s landscape, while the characters' problems seem small and temporary. It's a way of saying "this is what the era *sounded* like," rather than "this is what the characters are *feeling*."

column7: The recurring scenes of teenagers driving
column11: Schmidt attempts to interpret a specific aspect of the constant driving using the concept of The Road Chronotope. According to this interpretation, the cars are ultimately revealed to be more than just transportation; they are unique spatio-temporal zones where social hierarchies are both reinforced (seniors hunting freshmen) and subverted (private confessions). The car is a mobile, liminal space where the narrative, freed from static locations, truly unfolds.
column12: Let's break down this idea. "Chronotope" is a fancy term from theorist Mikhail Bakhtin that just means how time and space are represented together in a story. Scholar Schmidt applies this to the cars in *Dazed and Confused*. Think about how much of the movie happens in cars. They aren't just for getting from A to B. Schmidt argues that each car is its own little world with its own rules. It's a "Road Chronotope." Inside the car, characters can have deep conversations, escape their parents, or plan their next move. It's a private space that's also public and constantly moving. The car is where the film's time and space merge to create meaning, becoming the essential stage for the story.

column4: Holloway, Carol. "‘Alright, Alright, Alright’: Nostalgia, Irony, and the Performance of the Past." Film Quarterly 65, no. 3 (2012): 58-69.
column7: The film's overall aesthetic and tone
column11: Holloway attempts to interpret a specific aspect of the film's 1970s setting using the concept of Reflective Nostalgia. According to this interpretation, the film's aesthetic is ultimately revealed to be not a simple, celebratory recreation of the past (restorative nostalgia), but a self-aware examination of the act of remembering itself, complete with its contradictions, anxieties, and melancholic undertones. It lingers on the ache of longing, not just the good times.
column12: Most movies about the past try to make you feel like you're really there, in a "good old days" kind of way. Theorist Svetlana Boym calls this "restorative nostalgia." But she has another concept: "reflective nostalgia." This is when a work doesn't try to rebuild the past perfectly but instead focuses on the feeling of memory and loss itself. Scholar Holloway argues *Dazed and Confused* does the latter. It's not just a fun trip to the 70s. It's also sad and a little empty. The film isn't saying "the 70s were great!"; it's saying "remembering the 70s feels like this—a mix of fun, boredom, and a sense of something lost." It's about the feeling of looking back.

column4: Berger, Anne W. "Paddling Toward Manhood: Ritual Hazing and the Reproduction of Masculinity." JCMS: Journal of Cinema and Media Studies 48, no. 2 (2009): 103-125.
column7: The senior boys' hazing of incoming freshmen
column11: Berger attempts to interpret a specific aspect of the freshman hazing using the concept of Hegemonic Masculinity. According to this interpretation, the paddling ritual is ultimately revealed to be a violent performance through which a dominant, aggressive, and heterosexual model of masculinity is enforced upon the next generation. The complicity of even "good guys" like Pink demonstrates how pervasive and difficult this dominant structure is to escape.
column12: This analysis focuses on the intense hazing scenes. R.W. Connell, a sociologist, developed the idea of "hegemonic masculinity," which is the dominant, most socially accepted form of being a man in a given culture (usually tough, strong, heterosexual, etc.). Scholar Berger uses this idea to explain the hazing. The paddling isn't just random bullying. It's a ritual where the senior boys teach the freshmen "how to be men" according to this dominant, aggressive model. By participating, even a thoughtful character like Pink helps this system continue. column12: Why does it feel like nothing really "happens" in *Dazed and Confused*? Scholar Lefebvre explains this using an idea from philosopher Gilles Deleuze. Deleuze talked about two types of film images. The "movement-image" is what we see in most Hollywood movies—characters have clear goals and take action to achieve them (action films, romances). The "time-image," more common in European cinema, is different. It focuses on characters who drift, wait, and observe. The plot isn't the point. Lefebvre argues *Dazed and Confused* is a great example of the time-image. We are just watching these kids exist, experiencing boredom, random conversations, and the slow passage of a single day. The film asks us to think about time itself, not just what happens next.

column12: The big party at the end of the film happens at the "Moontower," a place away from parents, teachers, and rules. Scholar Cho argues the Moontower is a classic liminal space. Once there, the normal high school cliques (jocks, nerds, etc.) start to break down. This creates what Turner called "communitas"—a feeling of intense community and social bonding among people who are normally separate. For a few hours, everyone is just a teenager at a party, not defined by their social group, before the sun comes up and they have to go back to their regular lives.

Peterson argues that Linklater is doing a rhythmanalysis of 1970s teenage life. The film captures the specific pulse of being a teen in that time and place. It shows the recurring patterns: the slow, repetitive rhythm of cruising in a car, the sudden, chaotic rhythm of a fight or a party, and the long, quiet rhythm of just being bored. By focusing on these cycles instead of a big plot, the film feels more real and gives us a deeper understanding of that specific way of life.

Instead, our identities are often seen as a collage or a mix-and-match of different styles, ideas, and influences we pick up from culture—this is called "pastiche." Beuka argues Cher's closet is a perfect metaphor for this. Each morning, she doesn't just pick clothes; she literally assembles her identity for the day from a digital library of fashion pieces. See traces the history of the "Southern California girl" in movies, starting with characters like Gidget in the 50s/60s. She argues that Cher and her friends in Clueless are not a spontaneous phenomenon; they are the 1990s evolution of this long-standing stereotype. As she walks past the fountain, all the pieces click into place, and she realizes, "Oh my god, I love Josh." This isn't just a romantic plot point; it's the therapeutic climax of her character arc, where she finally understands herself, leading to her personal growth.

The rolling hills, sunny vineyards, and quaint wineries are presented in a way that makes them seem romantic, a little sad, and very cultured. This cinematic version of the valley became so powerful that it attracted a wave of tourism—the "Sideways effect"—from people wanting to live out the specific mood and fantasy the film created, demonstrating how movies can transform real-world locations into destinations.

In the film, he gets a message from Maya and goes to her door, leaving the audience with a sense of possibility. Stam argues that this change is a deliberate choice by director Alexander Payne to inject his own worldview—one of cautious optimism about human connection—into the story.

Scholar Timothy Corrigan argues that Sideways plays with these rules only to break them. He calls it an "anti-road movie." Instead of finding themselves or escaping their problems, Miles and Jack's trip is mostly a series of detours, mistakes, and embarrassments. They drive around a lot, but they don't really get anywhere emotionally or psychologically. They end up right back where they started, with the same problems. column12: Why is Miles so obsessed with Pinot Noir? Scholar Scott Lash uses the idea of "cultural capital," developed by sociologist Pierre Bourdieu, to explain. In this view, Miles's passionate speech about Pinot being "thin-skinned, temperamental, and in need of care" is a way of showing off his sophisticated knowledge. He's using wine expertise as a currency to prove he is refined and intelligent. It's also how he connects with Maya, who speaks the same "language" of taste, and a metaphor for how he sees himself.

column12: This analysis looks at Sideways as a signature work of its director, Alexander Payne. Scholar Roy Grundmann argues that you can see Payne's unique style, or "auteurist signature," in the film's specific tone. Payne consistently makes films that are both funny and sad, often at the same time. He pokes fun at his characters' weaknesses and bad decisions, but he never treats them with pure contempt. There's always an underlying sympathy and understanding—a humanism—that makes us care about them despite their flaws. This blend of sharp satire and genuine empathy is the key to understanding Sideways and Payne's other films.

Freud distinguished "mourning" (healthy grieving) from "melancholia" (a pathological state where a person's anger at their loss gets turned inward, leading to self-hatred). Silverman argues that Miles is melancholic. By drinking the fancy wine in a trashy way, he's not just sad; he's punishing himself. The act symbolizes his own feelings of worthlessness after his divorce and professional rejection.

Instead of making us feel exactly what the characters are feeling, the music creates a bit of distance, highlighting the absurdity and humor of their mid-life crises.

column12: This analysis uses a key idea from the philosopher Giorgio Agamben. He described a figure from ancient Roman law called "Homo Sacer," a person who was banned from society and could be killed by anyone, but could not be used in a religious sacrifice. This person had 'bare life'—they were just a biological body without any rights or protections. Raipol argues that the refugees ('fugees') in the Bexhill camp are modern-day Homo Sacer. The camp is a 'state of exception,' a lawless zone where the government suspends normal rights. He argues that *The Incredibles* is a perfect example of this formula. It takes on very adult ideas, like feeling useless at your job or going through a midlife crisis, but presents them in a way that's still exciting and funny for kids. This ability to be both emotionally complex for adults and entertaining for children, all while looking amazing, is the signature "Pixar Touch." The film isn't just a one-off success; it's a masterful execution of the studio's unique brand of storytelling.

According to this interpretation, Belle's agency is ultimately revealed to be a superficial masquerade that contains her desires within acceptable patriarchal structures; her intelligence leads not to liberation but to a "better" domestic partnership, reinforcing the idea that a woman's ultimate fulfillment is through marriage.
column12: This analysis explores how Belle, despite seeming like a modern, independent woman, might actually represent a subtle, newer form of sexism called "postfeminism." The idea is that the film gives Belle traits we admire, like her love for reading and her rejection of the brutish Gaston. However, the scholar argues this is a surface-level empowerment. Instead of using her intelligence to build a life for herself outside of traditional expectations, her journey's ultimate goal is still finding a suitable husband. Her "choice" to love the Beast simply domesticates him, making him a better partner. So, while she appears to have agency, the film subtly reinforces the old-fashioned idea that a woman's main purpose and happiness are found in marriage, just with a more refined and intelligent partner.

column12: This scholar examines Gaston not just as a simple villain, but as an example of what's called "hegemonic masculinity." This term refers to the dominant, most socially accepted form of manhood in a given culture, which often involves being strong, aggressive, and emotionally reserved. The analysis points out how Gaston is initially celebrated by the entire town for these very qualities—he's handsome, a great hunter, and confident. However, the film slowly reveals that these same traits make him arrogant, cruel, and unable to accept rejection. By making the most "manly" man in town the villain, the film is subtly criticizing this specific, toxic version of masculinity, suggesting that true strength lies not in biceps and bluster, but in kindness and vulnerability, as seen in the Beast's transformation.

According to this interpretation, the West Wing is ultimately revealed to be a physical manifestation of the Beast's repressed trauma and primal rage—an unsymbolizable, terrifying space that lies outside the Symbolic order of the rest of the castle, which Belle must confront to understand his psyche.
column12: Using ideas from the psychoanalyst Jacques Lacan, this analysis looks at the West Wing as more than just a forbidden room. Lacan had a concept called "the Real," which isn't reality as we know it, but the raw, chaotic, and often traumatic core of our being that's impossible to put into words or symbols. The scholar argues that the West Wing is a physical representation of the Beast's "Real." The rest of the castle is orderly and follows rules (the "Symbolic order"), but the West Wing is a mess of broken furniture, clawed-up paintings, and raw emotion. It's the place where the Beast's pain, shame, and rage live. By forbidding Belle from entering, he's trying to hide this traumatic part of himself. Her entering it and seeing the enchanted rose is a crucial step in her understanding his deep-seated trauma.

column12: This analysis focuses on the famous ballroom scene from a technological and aesthetic perspective. The scholar argues that this scene is a prime example of "cinematic spectacle"—a moment in a film designed to be so visually breathtaking that it becomes an experience in itself, separate from the narrative. What made this scene revolutionary was Disney's use of a new computer system (CAPS). It allowed them to create a vast, detailed 3D ballroom and have the camera swoop and fly through it, while the hand-drawn 2D characters of Belle and the Beast danced within that space. This fusion of techniques was groundbreaking. The scene's purpose was not just to show the characters falling in love, but also to show off Disney's incredible technical skill and create a moment of pure visual wonder for the audience.

column11: Horowitz attempts to interpret the enchanted servants' dual nature as both objects and laborers using the Marxist concept of Alienated Labor. According to this interpretation, the objects are ultimately revealed to be a metaphor for a workforce whose humanity has been stripped away by their master. Their curse physically transforms them into the tools of their trade, and their collective desire to become human again symbolizes the struggle of the working class to reclaim their identity from their role in the production process.
column12: This analysis uses ideas from Karl Marx to examine the enchanted objects like Lumière and Cogsworth. The core concept is "alienated labor," which describes how workers in a capitalist system can feel disconnected from their work and from their own humanity, becoming mere cogs in a machine. The scholar argues that the film makes this metaphor literal: the servants have been physically turned into the objects of their labor (a candelabra, a clock, a teapot). They are no longer people but things. Their entire existence is defined by their function in the castle. The song "Be Our Guest" is seen not just as a welcoming gesture, but as a performance of their labor. Their desperate wish to break the spell and become human again is interpreted as a symbolic struggle of workers to overcome this alienation and be seen as people rather than just their jobs.

column12: This analysis explores the character of LeFou through the lens of Queer Theory, focusing on the idea of "coding" and "camp." Since mainstream films of the time wouldn't explicitly show a gay character, artists would sometimes use "codes"—subtle hints like flamboyant behavior or specific ways of speaking—that LGBTQ+ audiences might recognize. The scholar argues LeFou is such a coded character. His name literally means "the fool," and his over-the-top, theatrical devotion to Gaston is interpreted as a form of "camp"—a style that finds value in exaggeration and artifice. His entire performance of admiration for Gaston's manliness is so extreme that it almost becomes a parody of heterosexual hero-worship, allowing for a subtextual reading of his desire for Gaston.

column12: This scholar analyzes the opening song, "Belle," using a concept from musical theater studies known as the "'I Want' Song." This is typically an early number in a musical where the main character sings about their deepest desires and what's missing from their life. The analysis shows how perfectly the song "Belle" fits this mold. Through the lyrics, we learn everything we need to know about her: the town thinks she's odd, she feels like an outsider, and she yearns for "adventure in the great wide somewhere." It's a very efficient storytelling tool. In just a few minutes of music, the film establishes Belle’s personality, her main conflict with her surroundings, and what will motivate all of her actions for the rest of the movie. It's the engine that drives the entire plot forward.

Unlike the fairy tale's focus on Belle's internal moral development, the film creates a clear-cut male antagonist, shifting the narrative from a quiet moral fable to a conventional good-versus-evil romantic action plot, better suited to modern blockbuster conventions.

In the original story, the conflict is mostly internal for Belle; she has to learn to see past the Beast's appearance. There is no external villain trying to kill him. The scholar argues that by inventing Gaston, Disney made an "ideological adaptation"—they didn't just change the plot, they changed the story's core message and structure. The conflict is no longer internal and moral, but external and physical. It becomes a simple story of a good guy (the reformed Beast) versus a bad guy (Gaston) fighting over a girl. This change transforms the quiet, introspective fairy tale into an action-filled romance, which is more typical of a modern Disney blockbuster.

column7: Paul's direct address to the camera
column11: Rushton interprets Paul's wink to the camera using the Brechtian Verfremdungseffekt. The act shatters the diegetic illusion, forcing viewers to abandon emotional immersion and critically reflect on their role as spectators. According to this interpretation, the Target Object is revealed to be a mechanism that exposes the audience's voyeuristic complicity in the on-screen violence, transforming passive entertainment into an uncomfortable ethical self-examination.
column12: Think of how you usually get lost in a movie's story. Bertolt Brecht, a German playwright, wanted to stop this. He created the 'Verfremdungseffekt' or 'alienation effect'—techniques that constantly remind you you're watching a performance, not reality. Rushton argues that when Paul winks at us, Haneke is using this exact technique. It's a jolt that pulls us out of the story. Instead of just feeling scared for Anna, we are forced to think, "Why am I watching this? Do I enjoy this violence?" The wink makes us aware of our own position as viewers and questions our desire to see suffering as entertainment. It turns the film from a simple thriller into a critique of its own audience.

column4: Wood, Robin. "Don't Look! The Repression of Violence in 'Funny Games'." Jump Cut: A Review of Contemporary Media, no. 43 (2000).
column7: The off-screen murder of Georgie
column11: Wood analyzes the off-screen murder of Georgie using the concept of the Unseen. By denying the audience visual access to the violent act and focusing on Anna's reaction, the film critiques the spectacle of violence common in horror. According to this interpretation, the Target Object is revealed to be a strategy to force the viewer's imagination to conjure a more horrific image than could be shown, implicating them in the act and highlighting the ethical bankruptcy of cinematic violence as entertainment.
column12: Robin Wood suggests that what we *don't* see is often more powerful and disturbing than what we do. In most horror movies, you'd see the violent act in graphic detail. Haneke does the opposite. We hear a gunshot, but the camera stays on Anna's face. Wood argues this is a deliberate choice. By refusing to show us the violence, Haneke makes us imagine it. Our own minds create the horror, which can be far more personal and terrifying. This technique avoids turning violence into a cool, consumable spectacle and makes us uncomfortable accomplices, as we are the ones "producing" the gruesome image in our heads. It's a powerful critique of our appetite for on-screen gore.

column11: Wheatley examines the rewind scene through the lens of meta-cinematic rupture. When Paul uses a remote control to reverse the film's action and prevent Anna's successful counter-attack, the film's internal logic is broken. According to this interpretation, the Target Object is revealed to be Haneke's ultimate authorial intervention, demonstrating that the narrative is a constructed artifice designed to deny the audience the catharsis they expect from genre cinema and to underscore the director's didactic, controlling purpose.
column12: "Meta-cinema" means the film is aware of itself as a film. Catherine Wheatley points to the rewind scene as a prime example. In a normal movie, the story follows its own rules. But here, Paul grabs a TV remote and literally rewinds the movie itself to undo Anna shooting Peter. This is a massive "rupture" or break in the film's reality. Wheatley argues this is Haneke the director showing his hand. He's telling us, "I am in complete control here. You are not getting the happy ending or the moment of revenge you crave." It shatters our illusion of a self-contained story and forces us to confront the fact that we are watching a deliberate, manipulated construction designed to teach us a lesson about our consumption of violent media.

column7: The killers' lack of motivation and shifting identities
column11: Finke interprets the killers' fluid, motiveless identities using the concepts of postmodern pastiche and simulacra. Paul and Peter offer contradictory backstories and behave like characters playing roles from different films, lacking any authentic psychological depth. According to this interpretation, the Target Object is revealed to be a representation of evil as a depthless surface, a copy without an original, reflecting a postmodern condition where meaning and motivation are detached from action, existing only as recycled media tropes.
column12: Jean Baudrillard, a postmodern thinker, talked about "simulacra"—copies of things that no longer have an original in the real world (think of a Disneyland castle). Johannes Finke applies this idea to the killers, Paul and Peter. They give multiple, fake backstories. Finke argues they aren't real characters with a real motive. Instead, they are a "pastiche," a collage of killer-types we've seen in other movies. They are simulacra of movie villains. Their evil isn't rooted in psychology; it's rooted in the language of cinema itself. This makes them terrifying because their violence is meaningless, a performance of violence detached from any human reason.

column11: Sharrett analyzes the opening scene's audio collision using the concept of a diegetic/non-diegetic sound clash. The family's serene world, defined by diegetic classical music, is abruptly shattered by the non-diegetic, brutal metal music of the opening credits. According to this interpretation, the Target Object is revealed to be a formalist declaration of intent, signaling the film's assault on bourgeois comfort and the viewer's generic expectations, aurally enacting the violent intrusion that will define the narrative.
column12: In film, "diegetic" sound is part of the story's world (like a character turning on a radio), while "non-diegetic" sound is outside it (like the film's soundtrack). Christopher Sharrett points to the opening scene where these two clash. The family peacefully enjoys their classical music—this is diegetic. Suddenly, the screen freezes and we're hit with loud, abrasive heavy metal. This is non-diegetic. Sharrett explains this is Haneke's mission statement. He is aurally demonstrating what the film is about to do: violently tear apart the peaceful world of this family (and the audience) with a brutal, external force. The sound itself performs the home invasion.

column4: Fisher, Mark. "The Politics of the 'Glacial'." Sight & Sound 18, no. 3 (2008): 28-32.
column7: The prolonged, single-take shot of the living room after Georgie's murder
column11: Fisher interprets the static, ten-minute long take after Georgie's death using his concept of the "glacial gaze." The camera's refusal to move, cut, or offer emotional cues creates an affectless, detached perspective, denying the audience traditional cinematic mourning or catharsis. According to this interpretation, the Target Object is revealed to be an aesthetic strategy that uses the long take to produce a cold, clinical horror that forces a confrontation with the duration and banal reality of suffering.
column12: Film critic Mark Fisher described Haneke's style as "glacial"—meaning it's cold, slow, and emotionally distant. He points to the incredibly long, 10-minute shot of the living room after the son has been killed. A normal film would use editing, close-ups, and music to guide our feelings. Haneke does none of that. His camera just sits there, like a cold, uncaring observer. Fisher argues this is a deliberate technique. It frustrates our desire for drama and action. Instead of a thrilling or sad scene, we are forced to sit with the raw, boring, and agonizing *duration* of the aftermath. It's a way of representing trauma that feels more real and disturbing than any flashy, edited sequence could.
